title: The Country of the Blind
focus: the arrogance and loneliness of seeing differently

teacherSummary.text: Mountaineer Nunez falls into an isolated Andean valley whose people have been blind for fifteen generations and no longer believe in sight. He expects 'In the Country of the Blind the One-eyed Man is King' but is treated as a madman. He falls in love with Medina-saroté; the elders agree to the marriage if his eyes, thought to be diseased, are removed. On the morning of the operation he climbs out of the valley and lies smiling under the stars.

I read “In the Country of the Blind the One-eyed Man is King” slowly and put it in my own words: Nunez remembers the saying that a one-eyed man would be king among the blind. Next, craft. Why does Nunez repeat the proverb, and what does the story do with it? My answer: He assumes his sight will make him a ruler, but the villagers have built a life without sight; the story shows that the proverb is arrogant and wrong.

followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Wells overturns Nunez's belief that sight makes him superior. Useful evidence: “I come from the great world—where men have eyes and see” (The Country of the Blind, paragraph 55): His arrogance. Theme link: the valley wants to "cure" his difference. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
